summary: Accenture Labs authors (ASE '26 New Ideas track, 5 pages) argue that delegating work to coding agents removes the incidental learning developers used to get from effortful problem solving, and call the resulting gap between agent changes and developer understanding 'Knowledge Debt'. They propose six design principles (contextual, grounded, ambient, selective, adaptive, closed-loop) and describe SHIELD, a CrewAI multi-agent VS Code prototype on GPT-5.1. SHIELD reads telemetry that Claude Code is instructed to emit for each change (rationale, alternatives, confidence), triages teachable concepts against a per-developer Neo4j concept map, queues probe questions, generates microlearning, and runs a comprehension check afterwards. There is no evaluation: one illustrative walkthrough and unquantified internal stakeholder feedback.

claims.claim: Over-reliance on agentic coding causes skill atrophy and accumulating Knowledge Debt
claims.evidence: Rests entirely on cited external work (e.g. a controlled study reporting 17% lower comprehension with AI assistance) and analogies to GPS and spell-check. The paper collects no data of its own.

claims.claim: Incidental learning will not re-emerge on its own and must be designed back into developer-agent interaction
claims.evidence: Argued, not tested. No comparison of developers with and without any intervention.

claims.claim: SHIELD operationalizes the six principles and surfaces learning moments without disrupting developer flow
claims.evidence: §4.1 maps components to principles. Fig. 2 is one illustrative webhook-retry scenario. Flow, interruption cost, probe quality and learning are not measured; there is no user study.

claims.claim: The coding agent's own reasoning (rationale, alternatives considered, confidence) is the right signal for deciding what is teachable
claims.evidence: Stated as the 'Grounded' principle. The telemetry is self-reported by the agent through an instruction in its configuration file; its faithfulness to what the agent actually did, and the calibration of its confidence, are not checked.
One sentence about stakeholders inside the authors' organization; no numbers, protocol or participants.

patterns.note: The core proposal: an out-of-band probe queue, a microlearning feed tied to the specific change, a per-developer concept map to suppress already-known concepts, and a post-learning comprehension check. Nothing is compared against an alternative, not even a pilot. Other KB papers found LLM explanations alone did not improve comprehension (2607.08885, 2607.26375); SHIELD's untested probes and checks are the part that might differ.

Instruments the coding agent, through its configuration file, to write structured per-change telemetry (what changed, rationale, alternatives, confidence) to a file that a separate observer consumes. This depends on the agent complying, and faithfulness is not verified.

Six role agents (telemetry observer, orchestrator, teachability triage, probe generator, knowledge assessor, microlearning generator) on CrewAI. No comparison with a single agent or a simpler rule-based trigger.
A persistent per-developer concept map (Neo4j graph), cold-started from code the developer wrote themselves and updated by probe and check outcomes. Its accuracy is not evaluated.

methodology.sample: None; one illustrative scenario (webhook retry with exponential backoff)
methodology.models: GPT-5.1 for all SHIELD agents; Claude Code as the instrumented coding agent

standards.peer_review: Accepted to the ASE '26 New Ideas and Emerging Results track (5 pages)
standards.artifacts: None; the Data Availability statement says no datasets accompany the paper and no code link is given

biases.detail: Vision paper; empirical user studies are listed as future work.
The only demonstration is a single author-chosen walkthrough (Fig. 2).
'Knowledge Debt' renames the epistemic or comprehension debt the paper itself cites in related work; the difference claimed is the incidental-learning framing.
'Promising feedback' comes from unquantified demonstrations inside the authors' own organization.
Built on one model (GPT-5.1) and wired to one coding agent (Claude Code).
No prototype code, prompts or configuration released.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: SHIELD (authors' own prototype); uses Claude Code, GPT-5.1, CrewAI, Azure, Neo4j
coi.detail: A consulting firm presents its own prototype. It makes no quantitative performance claims that could be inflated; the only positive signal is internal stakeholder feedback.

verdict_reason: No evaluation of any kind. The design principles and SHIELD are unvalidated, the only demonstration is one illustrative walkthrough, and the reported feedback is internal and unquantified. The topic (skill safeguards for developers delegating to agents) is squarely in scope, but the paper is a design checklist, not evidence.
applicability: For the Java multi-repo team, whose new developers lack domain knowledge, the six principles are a usable checklist for an onboarding or learning mode. Tie explanations to the specific change, queue them out of band instead of blocking, fire selectively, skip concepts the developer already knows, and verify with a probe rather than counting delivery as success. The cheapest transferable piece is host-neutral: a line in the repo's agent rule file asking the agent to write a per-change record of rationale and alternatives, which doubles as a review and handoff artifact. Two cautions. First, other KB studies found that LLM explanations alone did not improve comprehension and could raise confidence, so if the team builds anything like this, the probe and comprehension-check loop is the part to pilot and measure, not the explanation feed. Second, the agent's self-reported 'confidence' and 'alternatives considered' should not be trusted as teachability signals without checks. The prototype needs a GPT-5.1, CrewAI, Neo4j and Azure stack and supports only Claude Code, which does not fit a host-neutral harness, and nothing is released.

conflicts_with.detail: A pre-registered experiment found that LLM-written explanatory comments did not improve programmers' accuracy in judging generated code, and low-quality explanations raised confidence. SHIELD assumes, without testing, that agent-derived explanations (microlearning) repay Knowledge Debt.

Users of an agent that explained its edits and offered per-file review still scored much lower on comprehension of their own code than users of a restricted snippet-only chatbot. This cuts against SHIELD's premise that surfacing the agent's own reasoning restores learning. SHIELD adds probes and comprehension checks, which that study did not test.
